title: Fundamentals of Testing
content:
1.1 WHAT IS TESTING?
Software testing is a set of activities to discover defects and evaluate the quality of software artifacts (work products). It involves both dynamic testing (executing software) and static testing (examining work products without execution).

• Typical Test Objectives (FL-1.1.1):
  1. Evaluating work products (requirements, user stories, designs, code)
  2. Triggering failures and finding defects
  3. Ensuring required coverage of test objects
  4. Reducing the risk of inadequate software quality
  5. Verifying whether specified requirements have been fulfilled
  6. Checking whether the test object complies with contractual, legal, or regulatory requirements
  7. Providing stakeholders with information to make informed decisions
  8. Building confidence in the quality of the software

• Testing vs. Debugging (FL-1.1.2):
  - Testing: Identifies failures (dynamic) or defects (static). It demonstrates whether the software meets requirements. Performed primarily by testers.
  - Debugging: The development activity that locates, analyzes, and fixes the defects causing observed failures. Performed primarily by developers.
  - Confirmation Testing (Re-testing): After debugging, testers re-test the scenario to confirm the defect was successfully resolved.


1.2 WHY IS TESTING NECESSARY?
• Value of Testing (FL-1.2.1):
  Software testing reduces the risk of operational failures, saves time and financial cost, protects brand reputation, and can prevent injury or loss of life in safety-critical systems.

• Testing and Quality Assurance (QA) (FL-1.2.2):
  - Quality Assurance (QA): Process-oriented activity focused on adhering to proper processes to ensure quality requirements will be met. QA is preventative.
  - Quality Control (QC): Product-oriented activity aimed at evaluating artifacts to identify defects. Testing is a major part of Quality Control.

• Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes (FL-1.2.3):
  - Human Error (Mistake): A person makes an error (e.g. misunderstands a requirement, makes a coding typo, works under time pressure).
  - Defect (Bug / Fault): The manifestation of the human error in a work product (e.g. flawed code, incorrect specification).
  - Failure: An event in which the system deviates from expected behavior during runtime (e.g. system crashes, wrong total calculated).
  - Root Cause: The fundamental reason why the error occurred (e.g. lack of training, ambiguous user story). Root cause analysis helps eliminate recurring defect patterns.
  Note: A defect does not always lead to a failure (e.g. dead code never executed).


1.3 THE SEVEN TESTING PRINCIPLES (FL-1.3.1)
1. Testing shows the presence, not the absence of defects:
   Testing proves defects exist, but cannot prove that zero defects remain.
2. Exhaustive testing is impossible:
   Testing every possible combination of inputs and preconditions is infeasible except in trivial cases. Use risk analysis and test techniques to prioritize.
3. Early testing saves time and money:
   Defects caught early in requirements or design are vastly cheaper to fix than defects discovered in production (Shift-Left principle).
4. Defects cluster together (Pareto Principle / 80-20 Rule):
   A small proportion of system modules usually contain the majority of defects discovered, or are responsible for most operational failures.
5. Tests wear out (The Pesticide Paradox):
   If identical tests are repeated without changes, they eventually stop finding new defects. Tests must be reviewed, updated, and supplemented with new test cases.
6. Testing is context dependent:
   A safety-critical medical device is tested differently than an e-commerce mobile web application or an internal reporting tool.
7. Absence-of-defects fallacy:
   Fixing all discovered defects does not ensure success if the system does not satisfy user needs or business goals.


1.4 TEST ACTIVITIES, TESTWARE, AND TEST ROLES
• Test Activities in the Test Process (FL-1.4.1):
  1. Test Planning: Defining objectives, scope, approach, schedule, resources, and risks.
  2. Test Monitoring and Control: Monitoring progress against the plan and taking corrective control actions.
  3. Test Analysis: Analyzing the test basis to identify testable features and test conditions ('what to test').
  4. Test Design: Transforming test conditions into detailed test cases and test data specifications ('how to test').
  5. Test Implementation: Preparing test environments, test suites, test scripts, and test data.
  6. Test Execution: Running manual or automated tests and logging actual results and defects.
  7. Test Completion: Consolidating test assets, reporting results (Test Summary Report), capturing lessons learned.

• Testware (FL-1.4.2):
  Work products created during testing: test plans, test conditions, test cases, test data, test execution schedules, defect reports, and test summary reports.

• Traceability (FL-1.4.3):
  Maintaining bidirectional traceability between the test basis, test conditions, test cases, test results, and defect reports enables impact analysis and coverage measurement.

• Test Roles (FL-1.4.4):
  - Testing Role: Focuses on test analysis, design, implementation, and execution.
  - Test Management Role: Focuses on test planning, monitoring, control, and completion reporting.


1.5 ESSENTIAL SKILLS AND GOOD PRACTICES
• Essential Tester Skills (FL-1.5.1): Domain knowledge, technical proficiency, curiosity, analytical thinking, skepticism, attention to detail, and constructive communication.
• Whole-Team Approach (FL-1.5.2): Quality is the responsibility of the whole team (developers, testers, product owners, operations), not just testers.
• Independence of Testing (FL-1.5.3): Levels of independence range from self-testing author (lowest) to developers reviewing peers, independent test team, and external test specialists (highest).

title: Testing Throughout the Software Development Lifecycle
content:
2.1 TESTING IN THE CONTEXT OF AN SDLC
• Relationship between Development and Testing (FL-2.1.1):
  For every software development activity, there must be a corresponding testing activity. Testing should begin early in parallel with development.

• Good Testing Practices across SDLC Models (FL-2.1.2):
  - Sequential Models (Waterfall, V-Model): Strict progression through phases. Test planning and design start early alongside the corresponding development phase.
  - Iterative and Incremental Models (Agile, Scrum, Kanban): Software is delivered in short iterations. Testing occurs continuously throughout every iteration.

• Test-Driven Approaches (FL-2.1.3):
  - Test-Driven Development (TDD): Developer writes automated unit tests first, writes minimal code to pass tests, then refactors.
  - Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD): Collaborative specification of acceptance tests before development begins.
  - Behavior-Driven Development (BDD): Defines expected behavior using domain language and Given/When/Then scenarios.

• DevOps and Testing (FL-2.1.4):
  DevOps integrates development and operations to shorten deployment cycles through automated CI/CD pipelines, automated regression suites, continuous testing, and fast feedback.

• Shift-Left Approach (FL-2.1.5):
  Moving testing activities earlier in the lifecycle (static analysis, requirements reviews, early test design). Benefits: lower defect cost, fewer regressions, faster delivery.

• Retrospectives and Process Improvement (FL-2.1.6):
  Held at the end of iterations/projects to evaluate what went well, what can be improved, and identify concrete actions to enhance quality and testing efficiency.


2.2 TEST LEVELS AND TEST TYPES
• The Four Test Levels (FL-2.2.1):
  1. Component Testing (Unit Testing):
     - Test Object: Individual software components (classes, modules, functions).
     - Test Basis: Detailed design, component specifications, code.
     - Defects: Logic flaws, incorrect calculations, boundary handling.
     - Responsibility: Typically performed by developers in development environments.

  2. Component Integration Testing:
     - Test Object: Interactions, APIs, and interfaces between integrated components.
     - Test Basis: Software architecture, interface specifications, API documentation.
     - Defects: Communication failures, protocol mismatches, data format errors.

  3. System Testing:
     - Test Object: The complete, integrated system as a whole.
     - Test Basis: System requirements specifications, user stories, business processes, risk reports.
     - Defects: End-to-end workflow failures, system-level performance/security issues, functional deviations.
     - Responsibility: Typically independent test teams.

  4. Acceptance Testing:
     - Test Object: The system evaluated against user needs, business requirements, and operational readiness.
     - Test Basis: User requirements, business processes, regulations, contractual requirements.
     - Forms: User Acceptance Testing (UAT), Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT), Contractual/Regulatory testing, Alpha and Beta testing.

• The Four Test Types (FL-2.2.2):
  1. Functional Testing: Evaluates WHAT the system does (functions, features, business flows).
  2. Non-Functional Testing: Evaluates HOW WELL the system behaves according to ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics (performance efficiency, usability, security, reliability, maintainability, portability).
  3. Black-Box Testing: Specification-based; tests inputs and outputs without reference to internal structure.
  4. White-Box Testing: Structure-based; derives tests from source code, architecture, or internal logic.

• Confirmation Testing vs. Regression Testing (FL-2.2.3):
  - Confirmation Testing (Re-testing): Tests the specific defect fix to verify that the failure no longer occurs.
  - Regression Testing: Tests unchanged areas of the software to verify that modifications have not introduced unintended defects. Regression test suites are prime candidates for automation.


2.3 MAINTENANCE TESTING (FL-2.3.1, FL-2.3.2)
• Triggers for Maintenance Testing:
  1. Modifications (enhancements, defect fixes, corrective patches)
  2. Upgrades or migrations (platform changes, database upgrades, OS migration)
  3. Retirement / Decommissioning (archiving data, migration to replacement system)

• Impact Analysis:
  Evaluating the changes to determine potential consequences and identify areas affected. Determines the required scope of regression testing.

title: Static Testing
content:
3.1 STATIC TESTING BASICS
• Examinable Work Products (FL-3.1.1):
  Almost any work product can be examined by static testing: requirements specifications, user stories, architecture/design documents, source code, testware (test plans, test cases), user manuals, contracts, and web pages.

• Value of Static Testing (FL-3.1.2):
  - Detects defects directly (rather than observing failures during execution).
  - Finds defect types difficult to detect dynamically: unreachable/dead code, inconsistent requirements, security vulnerabilities, design flaws, maintainability deficiencies.
  - Dramatically reduces rework and total lifecycle costs by catching defects early.

• Static vs. Dynamic Testing (FL-3.1.3):
  - Static: Examines artifacts without executing code; finds defects directly; applicable to non-executable artifacts.
  - Dynamic: Executes code; identifies failures; requires an executable build and test environment.


3.2 FEEDBACK AND THE REVIEW PROCESS
• Early Stakeholder Feedback (FL-3.2.1):
  Early reviews prevent misunderstandings, clarify requirements early, align expectations, and foster collaboration across business and technical teams.

• Review Process Activities (FL-3.2.2):
  1. Planning: Defining scope, review type, objectives, estimating effort, selecting participants.
  2. Review Initiation: Distributing artifacts, explaining objectives, checking entry criteria.
  3. Individual Review: Reviewers independently examine the work product, note potential defects, questions, and observations.
  4. Communication and Analysis: Meeting or collaborative session to analyze logged issues, evaluate severity, and decide review outcome.
  5. Fixing and Reporting: Author fixes confirmed defects; facilitator/leader verifies fixes against exit criteria; metrics reported.

• Roles in a Formal Review (FL-3.2.3):
  - Author: Creates the work product under review; responsible for fixing confirmed defects.
  - Management: Allocates resources, schedules reviews, monitors review cost-effectiveness.
  - Facilitator (Moderator): Ensures review process is followed, chairs discussions, mediates disagreements.
  - Review Leader: Organizes the review, coordinates schedules, ensures participants are prepared.
  - Reviewer: Subject matter experts who inspect the artifact and identify defects.
  - Scribe (Recorder): Accurately records defect logs, decisions, and action items during discussions.

• Review Types from Informal to Formal (FL-3.2.4):
  1. Informal Review: No formal process, undocumented defect logging (e.g. peer check, buddy review).
  2. Walkthrough: Author-led presentation; primary goals are learning, gaining understanding, and finding defects.
  3. Technical Review: Peer-led evaluation by qualified technical experts; focuses on technical integrity and standards compliance.
  4. Inspection: The most formal review type; led by trained facilitator; strict entry/exit criteria, checklists, formal defect logging, metrics collection, and formal follow-up.

• Review Techniques (FL-3.2.5):
  - Ad hoc: Reviewers read without specific guidance.
  - Checklist-based: Systematic verification against documented checklists of common defects.
  - Scenarios and Dry Runs: Reviewers step through realistic usage scenarios.
  - Role-based: Reviewers evaluate from specific stakeholder viewpoints (e.g. system admin, security engineer).
  - Perspective-based: Reviewers simulate different stakeholder perspectives (user, developer, tester); highest defect detection rate.

• Success Factors for Reviews (FL-3.2.6):
  Clear objectives, appropriate review type, right participants with dedicated time, small chunks examined, checklists used, management support, and a blameless culture focused on quality improvement.

title: Test Analysis and Design
content:
4.1 TEST TECHNIQUES OVERVIEW (FL-4.1.1)
The purpose of test techniques is to derive test conditions, test cases, and test data from the test basis. Techniques are categorized into:
• Black-Box (Specification-Based): Based on requirements, use cases, or user stories without knowing internal code structure.
• White-Box (Structure-Based): Based on internal software structure, architecture, or code.
• Experience-Based: Based on the knowledge, intuition, and experience of testers and users.
• Collaboration-Based: Derived through collaborative discussions among cross-functional team members.


4.2 BLACK-BOX TEST TECHNIQUES
4.2.1 EQUIVALENCE PARTITIONING (EP) (FL-4.2.1 K3)
• How Equivalence Partitioning Works:
  Inputs and outputs are divided into partitions (equivalence classes) where all values in a partition are expected to be processed in the same way. Testing one representative value from each partition tests that whole group.

• Partition Categories:
  - Continuous Ranges (e.g. Allowed Age 18 to 65): Creates 1 valid partition (18 to 65) and 2 invalid partitions (less than 18, greater than 65).
  - Discrete / Choice Options (e.g. Credit Card, PayPal, Cash): Each allowed choice is 1 valid partition, plus 1 invalid partition for unrecognized options.

• Core Rules for Designing Test Cases:
  - Valid Partitions Can Be Combined: A single test case can combine valid inputs from multiple fields at once to minimize total test count.
  - Never Combine Invalid Values (Defect Masking): Every invalid partition must be tested in its own separate test case with all other inputs set to valid values. Combining invalid inputs causes one defect to hide another!
  - 100% EP Coverage: Achieved when tests exercise every identified partition (both valid and invalid) at least once.

4.2.2 BOUNDARY VALUE ANALYSIS (BVA) (FL-4.2.2 K3)
• Why Test Boundaries:
  Defects cluster at the extreme boundaries between partitions due to off-by-one errors or comparison mistakes (such as typing '<' instead of '<='). BVA specifically targets values at and near these edges.

• 2-Value BVA (CTFL v4.0 Standard):
  Tests 2 values per boundary: the exact boundary value and its closest immediate neighbor just outside the boundary.
  - For a valid range [10, 50], test 9 (just below min, invalid), 10 (min, valid), 50 (max, valid), 51 (just above max, invalid) → 4 test values.

• 3-Value BVA (Safety-Critical Systems):
  Tests 3 values per boundary: just below, exactly on, and just above the boundary.
  - Used in high-risk domains where internal boundary transitions must be rigorously verified.

• 100% BVA Coverage:
  Achieved when tests exercise every identified boundary value at least once.

4.2.3 DECISION TABLE TESTING (FL-4.2.3 K3)
• When to Use Decision Tables:
  Ideal for testing complex business logic where system outcomes depend on combinations of several conditions (inputs).
  - Condition Stubs: List all input conditions that can be True or False.
  - Action Stubs: List the possible system actions or outputs.
  - Rules (Columns): Each column defines a specific combination of conditions and the corresponding actions.

• Key Principles:
  - The Power of 2: Every True/False condition doubles the number of possible rules (2 conditions = 4 rules, 3 conditions = 8 rules, 4 conditions = 16 rules).
  - Don't Care (-) Entries: When a condition does not affect the outcome for a rule, it is marked as '-'. Each dash doubles the number of underlying rules covered by that single rule.
  - Table Completeness: A decision table is complete when all possible combinations are accounted for.

4.2.4 STATE TRANSITION TESTING (FL-4.2.4 K3)
• Stateful System Behavior:
  Used when system responses depend not only on current inputs, but also on past events and current internal state.
  - States: Conditions or modes in which the system rests (e.g. Logged Out, Shopping, Checkout).
  - Transitions: Changes from one state to another triggered by events.
  - Guard Conditions: Prerequisites that must be satisfied for a transition to occur.

• Levels of State Coverage:
  - All-States Coverage: Tests visit every state at least once.
  - 0-Switch (Transition) Coverage: Tests execute every valid transition at least once (Standard ISTQB target).
  - 1-Switch Coverage: Tests pairs of consecutive transitions (Transition 1 → Transition 2).
  - Negative Testing: Attempting invalid events that should be rejected in a given state.


4.3 WHITE-BOX TEST TECHNIQUES
4.3.1 STATEMENT TESTING & STATEMENT COVERAGE (FL-4.3.1 K2)
• What It Tests:
  Measures the percentage of executable source code statements executed by the test suite.
  - Statement Coverage = (Executable Statements Executed / Total Executable Statements) × 100%.

4.3.2 BRANCH TESTING & BRANCH COVERAGE (FL-4.3.2 K2)
• What It Tests:
  Measures the percentage of decision outcomes (both True and False branches of decision points like if-statements and loops) executed by the tests.
  - Branch Coverage = (Decision Outcomes Exercised / Total Decision Outcomes (Branches)) × 100%.
  - Every binary decision point has 2 branches (True branch and False branch): Total Decision Outcomes (Branches) = 2 × number of decisions.
  - The Golden Subsumption Rule: 100% Branch Coverage ALWAYS guarantees 100% Statement Coverage. 100% Statement Coverage DOES NOT guarantee 100% Branch Coverage!

4.3.3 CYCLOMATIC COMPLEXITY (FL-4.3.2 K2)
• What It Tells You:
  Measures the structural complexity of code and calculates the minimum number of test cases needed to achieve 100% branch coverage.
  - Quick Rule: Cyclomatic Complexity = Number of decision points (if, while, for) + 1.

4.3.4 VALUE OF WHITE-BOX TESTING (FL-4.3.3 K2)
• Identifies unreachable (dead) code, logic gaps, unhandled conditions, and security flaws directly inside the implementation.


4.4 EXPERIENCE-BASED TEST TECHNIQUES
4.4.1 ERROR GUESSING (FL-4.4.1 K2):
• Anticipating defects based on tester intuition, past defect patterns, and common programming pitfalls (e.g. division by zero, null values, empty fields, character overflow).

4.4.2 EXPLORATORY TESTING (FL-4.4.2 K2):
• Simultaneous learning, test design, and test execution without pre-written test cases.
• Test Charter: Outlines the objective, scope, and target feature of the test session.
• Time-Boxing: Sessions run within fixed time windows (typically 60 to 120 minutes).
• Session-Based Test Management (SBTM): Structured approach including charter, session metrics, defect logs, and debriefing.

4.4.3 CHECKLIST-BASED TESTING (FL-4.4.3 K2):
• Testers execute tests guided by documented checklists derived from experience, industry standards, or previous defects.


4.5 COLLABORATION-BASED TEST APPROACHES
4.5.1 COLLABORATIVE USER STORIES (FL-4.5.1 K2):
• The 3 Cs Framework:
  1. Card: Physical or digital card capturing story title and description.
  2. Conversation: Continuous dialogue between Product Owner, Developers, and Testers.
  3. Confirmation: Acceptance criteria confirming when the story meets expectations.

4.5.2 ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA & GHERKIN (FL-4.5.2 K2):
• Clear criteria that must be satisfied for a user story to be accepted.
• Formatted using Gherkin syntax:
  - Given [initial precondition]
  - When [user action or event]
  - Then [expected system result]

4.5.3 ACCEPTANCE TEST-DRIVEN DEVELOPMENT (ATDD) (FL-4.5.3 K2):
• 4-Stage Collaborative Cycle: Discuss requirements → Distill acceptance tests → Develop code to pass tests → Demo to stakeholders.
• Promotes defect prevention before coding begins and produces automated regression tests.

title: Managing the Test Activities
content:
5.1 TEST PLANNING
5.1.1 PURPOSE AND CONTENT OF A TEST PLAN (FL-5.1.1 K2):
• Purpose: Defines the scope, approach, objectives, resources, schedule, and risks of testing activities. Communicates the testing roadmap to all stakeholders.
• Test Strategy vs. Test Plan:
  - Test Strategy: High-level organizational or program document defining generic test approaches, levels, and tools. Long-lasting across multiple projects.
  - Test Plan: Project-specific document defining operational activities, dates, personnel, environments, and deliverables.

5.1.2 CONTRIBUTION TO ITERATION AND RELEASE PLANNING (FL-5.1.2 K1):
• Testers participate in backlog refinement, story sizing, identifying testability risks, estimating test effort, and planning automation.

5.1.3 ENTRY AND EXIT CRITERIA (FL-5.1.3 K2):
• Entry Criteria (Definition of Ready - DoR): Prerequisites that must be met before testing activities begin (e.g. environment ready, smoke test passed, test basis available).
• Exit Criteria (Definition of Done - DoD): Prerequisites that must be satisfied before testing can be declared complete (e.g. planned tests run, target coverage met, critical defects resolved, residual risks documented).

5.1.4 TEST ESTIMATION TECHNIQUES (FL-5.1.4 K2):
• Metrics-Based: Uses historical data from past projects (defect arrival rate, velocity, burn-down charts).
• Expert-Based: Relies on the experience of experts.
  - Wideband Delphi: Iterative consensus estimation technique by a group of experts.
  - Planning Poker: Collaborative estimation using Fibonacci cards in Agile teams.
• Three-Point Estimation (PERT):
  Combines three scenarios: Optimistic (best case), Most Likely (expected), and Pessimistic (worst case), giving the Most Likely estimate 4 times the weight of the extremes.

5.1.5 TEST CASE PRIORITIZATION (FL-5.1.5 K2):
• Orders test execution based on risk exposure, business value, technical dependencies, and quick feedback.

5.1.6 THE TEST PYRAMID (FL-5.1.6 K1):
• Recommended test suite proportion:
  - Broad Base: Fast, automated Unit (Component) tests.
  - Middle Layer: Integration and API tests.
  - Narrow Top: System, End-to-End, and UI tests.

5.1.7 TESTING QUADRANTS (FL-5.1.7 K1):
• Quadrant 1 (Technology-Facing, Supporting Team): Unit & component tests, automated.
• Quadrant 2 (Business-Facing, Supporting Team): Functional story tests, examples, automated or manual.
• Quadrant 3 (Business-Facing, Critiquing Product): Exploratory, usability, user acceptance (UAT), manual.
• Quadrant 4 (Technology-Facing, Critiquing Product): Performance, load, security, reliability, tool-driven.


5.2 RISK MANAGEMENT
5.2.1 PRODUCT RISK VS. PROJECT RISK (FL-5.2.1 K2):
• Product Risk: Risk related to software quality and functionality (e.g. incorrect calculations, security holes, slow performance, data loss).
• Project Risk: Risk related to project management and schedule (e.g. staff shortages, late delivery, scope creep, vendor failure).

5.2.2 PRODUCT RISK ANALYSIS (FL-5.2.2 K2):
• Risk Assessment: Evaluates Likelihood (probability of failure) and Impact (damage if it fails).
• Risk Exposure (Risk Level): Calculated by multiplying Likelihood by Impact. Used to rank and prioritize testing.

5.2.3 RISK-BASED TESTING (RBT) (FL-5.2.3 K2):
• Allocates testing effort where risk is highest. High-risk areas receive deeper test techniques, earlier execution, and experienced testers.


5.3 TEST MONITORING, TEST CONTROL, AND TEST COMPLETION
5.3.1 METRICS USED IN TESTING (FL-5.3.1 K2):
• Progress Metrics: % tests planned vs executed, % passed, failed, and blocked.
• Defect Metrics:
  - Defect Density: Number of defects found divided by the size of the software (e.g. per 1,000 lines of code).
  - Defect Detection Percentage (DDP): Percentage of total bugs found by testing before release compared to bugs found by users in production.
• Coverage Metrics: Requirements coverage percentage and code coverage (statement and branch).

5.3.2 TEST REPORTS (FL-5.3.2 K2):
• Test Progress Report: Issued periodically during testing to inform stakeholders of status, blockers, and risks.
• Test Summary Report: Issued at test completion summarizing results, coverage, metrics, deviations from plan, residual risks, and release readiness.

5.3.3 COMMUNICATING STATUS OF TESTING (FL-5.3.3 K2):
• Factual, objective, transparent communication tailored to the audience (executive vs technical).


5.4 CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT (FL-5.4.1 K2)
• Ensures all items of testware (test cases, scripts, data, plans) and test objects are uniquely identified, versioned, tracked for changes, and traceable to requirements.


5.5 DEFECT MANAGEMENT (FL-5.5.1 K3)
• Defect Lifecycle: New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retested/Verified → Closed (or Deferred/Rejected).
• Key Elements of a Good Defect Report:
  1. Unique Identifier and Title
  2. Date, Author, and Status
  3. Environment Details (OS, browser, build number)
  4. Exact Steps to Reproduce
  5. Expected Result vs Actual Result
  6. Severity (technical impact: Critical, Major, Minor)
  7. Priority (business urgency: High, Medium, Low)
  8. Attachments (screenshots, logs, traces)
  9. Root Cause and Fix Details

title: Test Tools
content:
6.1 TOOL SUPPORT FOR TESTING
• Classification of Test Tools (FL-6.1.1):
  1. Management of Testing and Testware: Test management tools, requirements management tools, defect tracking tools, configuration management tools, continuous integration tools.
  2. Static Testing Tools: Static analysis tools (linters, analyzers), review support tools.
  3. Test Design and Implementation: Model-based testing tools, test data generation tools, acceptance test tools (BDD/ATDD tools).
  4. Test Execution and Logging: Automated test execution frameworks (Selenium, Playwright, JUnit), unit test harnesses, test runners.
  5. Performance Measurement and Dynamic Analysis: Load/stress testing tools, performance monitoring tools, memory leak profilers.
  6. Specialized Tools: Usability evaluation tools, accessibility tools, security testing tools (DAST/SAST).

• Benefits of Test Automation (FL-6.1.2):
  - Reduces repetitive manual test effort
  - Enables faster, more frequent execution (critical in CI/CD pipelines)
  - High consistency and repeatability (eliminates human error in test execution)
  - Enables execution of tests that are virtually impossible manually (high-volume load testing, 24/7 stress tests)
  - Objective metrics collection (code coverage, execution duration)

• Risks of Test Automation (FL-6.1.2):
  - Unrealistic expectations regarding tool capabilities and ROI
  - High initial investment in tool acquisition, setup, and training
  - Significant ongoing maintenance effort when the application under test changes
  - Underestimating the effort needed to maintain test scripts and test data
  - Over-reliance on automation, neglecting human exploratory testing and usability


6.2 SUCCESS FACTORS FOR TOOLS
• Principles for Tool Selection (FL-6.2.1):
  - Assess organizational maturity, strengths, and weaknesses
  - Identify opportunities for tool support
  - Understand available technologies and tool compatibility with test objects
  - Evaluate tool vendors or open-source community support
  - Conduct a Proof of Concept (PoC) to verify compatibility and suitability
  - Perform Return on Investment (ROI) and cost-benefit analysis

• Pilot Projects for Introducing a Tool (FL-6.2.2):
  - Learn more details about the tool and assess how it fits with existing workflows
  - Decide on standard ways of using, managing, storing, and maintaining test assets
  - Assess whether the benefits will be achieved at reasonable cost
  - Evaluate metrics that should be collected and reported

• Success Factors for Tool Rollout (FL-6.2.3):
  - Rolling out the tool incrementally across the organization
  - Adapting and improving processes to fit tool usage
  - Providing adequate training, coaching, and mentoring to users
  - Establishing clear guidelines and naming conventions for testware
  - Continuously monitoring tool usage and collecting feedback for ongoing improvement
